Hook: On the fifteenth of July 2021, most American families with children received a payment they had never had before. Three hundred dollars for each child under six, two hundred and fifty for each child from six to seventeen, every month. The rest came at tax time: 3,600 dollars a year for a young child and 3,000 for an older one, even for families with no earnings at all, who had received little or nothing from the old credit. The payments came for six months. In January 2022 they stopped: the law that created them lapsed, and Congress did not renew it.

What happened to child poverty? On the Census Bureau's Supplemental Poverty Measure, which counts taxes and credits as income, the share of American children in poverty was 9.7 percent in 2020. In 2021 it fell to 5.2 percent, the lowest ever recorded, and the Census Bureau credited the child tax credit with much of the fall. In 2022, with the payments gone, it was 12.4. The official measure, which counts only cash income before taxes, barely moved: 16.0 to 15.3. How a policy looks can depend on how it is measured, a theme this part returns to.

Now a request lands on your desk. The Island's finance minister asks whether the Island should pay every family a monthly allowance for each child, on the American design of 2021, made permanent. What would it do, what would it cost, and how sure are you? Four pages, in two weeks. This part writes that memo, using only what the series has built: the models, the dials, the evidence, and the Island.

The question: a minister asks whether to pay a child allowance. What do you write? First, what exactly is proposed, and who it touches. Then how families will respond, and how we know. Then what it costs and what it is worth. And how sure we are, and what would change the advice.
Economics, Built. Part fifty: the policy memo.

Here is the plan. The question made answerable, and what the allowance does to a family's budget. The dials that matter, and your own advice before any analysis. The margins a textbook picture misses, the budget, and the three best pieces of evidence. The policy run on the Island, its value per dollar, who gains and who loses, and the uncertainty. And then the memo itself, how such memos are used and misused, and what nobody yet knows.
Question: Chapter one. The question made answerable.

A memo begins by pinning the question down, because a vague question gets a vague answer. What exactly is proposed? The old credit, as it stood from 2018 to 2020, paid up to two thousand dollars a child. But a family that earned little got only part of it: at most fourteen hundred dollars a child, and only fifteen cents for every dollar earned above twenty-five hundred. A family with no earnings got nothing. It came once a year, at tax time. The proposal is the 2021 design made permanent: thirty-six hundred dollars for each child under six and three thousand for each older child, the whole of it paid whatever the family earns, every month, with the extra phased out for the better off. How to pay for it is a separate decision, and the memo must keep it separate, because the answer can depend on it.

Who is touched? The memo is for the Island, so it is answered on the Island. The Island has 40,000 families with children. About a third are single parents, 35 percent, the rest couples. They have 74,118 children between them, about a third of them under six. Most families have one or two children; a few have four. And what matters most for how they respond: what the main earner could earn in a year if they worked, about twenty-eight thousand dollars for the median single parent and fifty-two thousand for the median couple, with a long spread on both sides. These people are simulated, as always on the Island, built loosely to resemble American families.

Through which channels does it work, and over what horizon? The money arrives in the family's budget at once. Over the following months parents decide whether and how much to work, which changes their earnings and the taxes and credits they pay and receive. Within the year those decide two of the memo's numbers: how many children are poor, and what the policy costs. And over decades, the children's own schooling, health and earnings, which may feed back into the budget. The markets touched are the labour market, the markets for what families buy, housing, and the government's own budget. Each number in the memo belongs to one horizon, and the memo should say which.

And what counts as an answer? First, the comparison: the allowance against the credit it replaces, not against doing nothing. Then child poverty, measured against the Island's own line: twenty-four thousand dollars a year for two adults and two children, more for bigger families and less for smaller ones. Work: how many parents stop working, or start. The cost, counting the credits paid and the change in taxes collected. The value: what families gain per dollar the government spends, the yardstick of Part forty-two. And who gains and who pays. With the policy, the people, the outcomes, the comparison and the horizon named, the question can be answered.
Market: Chapter two. The family's budget, before and after.

Before any economics, the arithmetic of one family. Take a single parent with two children, one under six and one older. Both systems keep the earned income tax credit, the EITC of Part forty-one: it rises with earnings to almost six thousand dollars, stays flat, then fades out above twenty thousand. The old child credit also rose with earnings: fifteen cents per dollar earned above twenty-five hundred, until it reached its full four thousand dollars once the family earned enough and owed enough tax. The allowance is flat: six thousand six hundred dollars from the first dollar, or from no dollar at all, fading only above seventy-five thousand.

Now subtract: what the allowance adds, at each level of earnings. A family with no earnings gains the whole 6,600 dollars. The gain shrinks as the old credit phases in, and in the middle it is twenty-six hundred dollars, the difference between the new amounts and the old two thousand a child. Above seventy-five thousand the extra fades, and above 127 thousand there is none. So the allowance gives the most to the families that earn the least: the gain is largest exactly where the old credit was smallest.

Put the credits into the family's budget line: income after taxes and credits, against earnings. The grey line is the old system. The parent's income rises faster than earnings at first, because both credits are phased in. The gold line is the allowance: higher everywhere, by most at the bottom. A parent who does not work had nothing from these credits before, and has 6,600 dollars now. Now the decision to work. Under the old credit, working at twenty thousand dollars added 28,504 dollars to the family's income, earnings plus both credits less a little tax. Under the allowance it adds 25,759: the 2,745 dollars of child credit that work used to earn now come anyway. The reward for working falls by about a tenth for this parent. That single number is where the memo's hardest disagreement begins.

Two effects, from the theory of Part thirty-eight. The income effect: the family has more money whether or not the parent works, and with more money some people choose to work less. And the end of the phase-in: the old credit paid fifteen cents for each dollar earned at the bottom, a reward for starting work that the allowance removes. In the middle nothing changes at the margin: the family has more, but an extra hour pays the same. Above seventy-five thousand, the phase-out takes five cents of each extra dollar, a small new tax. At the bottom both effects point towards less work. Theory gives the direction; only evidence can give the size.
PlayIt: Chapter four. Play it: your advice, before the analysis.

Before the analysis, your advice. Write it down now, because a memo is easier to bend towards what you already believe than to write honestly, and the only defence is to know what you believed before you looked. Yes, as designed. Yes, but keep a work requirement, so the payment still rises with earnings at the bottom. Yes, but smaller. Or no: spend the money another way. What you know so far: in 2021 the payments came while child poverty, on the measure that counts credits, fell from 9.7 to 5.2 percent, although other pandemic aid was flowing too. And for one family, a large gain at the bottom and a somewhat smaller reward for working. Choose.

And a forecast, which the Island will check. Under the old credit, 14.3 percent of the Island's children are below its poverty line. With the allowance, after families have responded, by how much will that fall? By less than a tenth, by a tenth to a quarter, by a quarter to two fifths, or by more than two fifths? Remember that the 2021 headline was a fall of almost half. Pause, and choose.

Both answers are kept. The forecast comes back in chapter eight, when the Island runs the policy, and the advice in chapter twelve, when the memo is written. If the memo ends up saying exactly what you believed before you started, that is not proof that you were wrong; but it is a reason to check it twice.
Margins: Chapter five. The margins the textbook misses.

Textbook pictures assume that everyone eligible for a payment receives it. They do not. A credit paid through the tax system reaches families that file a tax return, and the families with the lowest incomes are the most likely not to file at all, because they owe nothing. In 2021 the tax authority built a simplified portal for them. On the Island, if every family claims, child poverty under the allowance is 11.6 percent; if only eighty-five percent claim, it is 12.3. The cost falls too, from 1,473 dollars a child to 1,248: incomplete take-up saves money exactly by failing the families the policy is for. And the Island is generous here: it lets the families who miss out be chosen at random. In fact they are poorer than average, so the real loss would be larger.

Second, timing. The old credit arrived once a year, in a lump at tax time. For a family with savings that makes little difference. For a family living month to month, a monthly payment is a different thing: it arrives when the rent and the food bills do. The present bias of Part forty-five says the same from the other side: a large sum in March is easily spent by April. During the six months of 2021, the Census Bureau's surveys found families spending the payments most often on food, and then on school costs, clothing, rent and bills. The catch: monthly payments are based on last year's income and family, and when circumstances change, someone must bear the overpayments. If families repay them at tax time, the risk falls on those with the least slack; the 2021 law protected low-income families from most repayment, at a cost to the budget.

Third, labels and conditions. In the textbook a dollar is a dollar: money given for children frees money for anything else, so the label does nothing. But Part forty-nine showed that whose purse the money reaches matters: when Britain moved its child allowance from fathers' pay packets to mothers, spending on children's clothing rose. The name matters too: a child benefit, a tax credit and welfare are claimed by different people and spent in different ways, which the behavioural economics of Part forty-five calls mental accounting. And the condition: a work requirement protects the reward for work, at the price of missing the children whose parents cannot work, because of illness, disability or caring. Each of these margins moves the answer, and none appears in the textbook picture.
Economy: Chapter six. The budget and the wider economy.

First, the budget. On the Island the allowance costs 109 million dollars a year more than the old credit, about 1,473 dollars for each child, counting the credits paid and the change in taxes collected. Surprisingly, families' responses barely change the cost: the parents who stop working earned little, paid little tax and received the earned income credit, so the budget loses almost nothing when they stop, about 0.2 percent of the cost. Scaled to some seventy million American children, that is about 103 billion dollars a year: about a third of one percent of the country's income. Large in dollars, small against the economy.

Who pays? A memo must not hide this, because the answer can depend on it. There are three ways. Borrowing, which moves the bill to later taxpayers. A tax on top incomes. Or cutting other spending, whose cost is whatever that spending was doing. For the surtax, Part forty-one's tools give the price. With a top rate of forty percent and top incomes spread like American ones, raising a dollar of revenue costs top earners 1.11 dollars if their elasticity is 0.1, 1.33 at a quarter, and 1.67 at 0.4, because some of each new dollar of tax is lost to smaller reported incomes. That number, the marginal cost of public funds, returns in chapter nine, where it sits underneath the value of the allowance.

What else moves, beyond the families themselves? General equilibrium, in the language of Part nine. Prices: the allowance adds about half of one percent to what Americans spend, spread across the whole country. In Kenya, transfers far larger relative to local incomes moved local prices very little. Wages: if some parents leave work, those who stay may earn a little more, a small effect in the policy's own direction. Births: from 1988 Quebec paid up to eight thousand Canadian dollars for a birth, and Kevin Milligan found fertility rose, by up to a quarter among families eligible for the full amount. A smaller yearly payment per child is a weaker incentive, but not none, and Part forty-nine's quantity and quality says what it might do. And the long run: what the money does for children's health, schooling and later earnings, which is also the budget's biggest unknown, because healthier, better-educated adults pay more tax. The next chapter is the evidence.
Evidence: The evidence. A memo should rest on the best few designs, each with what it identifies, and an honest word on whether it transfers to the case at hand. On poverty and work, two. First, America's own monthly payments of 2021. Elizabeth Ananat and her co-authors compared parents, who received them, with adults without children, who did not, before and after July. They found employment effects very small, of either sign, and statistically insignificant, including for parents in the range where the old credit had rewarded work. Second, Canada's Child Benefit of 2016, larger and permanent. Michael Baker, Derek Messacar and Mark Stabile compared families by how much their benefit rose. By 2018 poverty was about 11 percent lower among single mothers and 17 percent lower among couples, with no sign that parents worked less, on either margin.

The long run needs a different kind of evidence, because it takes a generation to arrive. Anna Aizer and her co-authors found the files of America's first welfare programme, the Mothers' Pensions of 1911 to 1935, and compared the sons of mothers who were accepted with the sons of mothers who applied and were turned down, 16,000 boys in all. The sons of accepted mothers lived about a year longer, had a third of a year more schooling, and earned more as adults. Kevin Milligan and Mark Stabile used Canadian benefits that differed across provinces, years and family types. Children whose families could get more had higher test scores, and their mothers better health and mental health. This is where most of an allowance's value may lie, and it is where the evidence is oldest, most indirect and thinnest.

And a counterpoint the memo must answer, not ignore. In 2021 Kevin Corinth, Bruce Meyer, Matthew Stadnicki and Derek Wu simulated a permanent American allowance, with participation elasticities from the mainstream of the labour literature, applied to the end of the phase-in and to the income the allowance adds. About 1.5 million working parents, 2.6 percent, would leave work, and child poverty would fall by at most 22 percent, not by the half that the static arithmetic suggests. This is not a measurement: it is a model, with elasticities borrowed from other settings. But it asks the right question, the one the 2021 experience cannot answer: what would a permanent policy do, once families had years to adjust?

Do these transfer to the Island's permanent allowance? Ask four questions of each. The 2021 payments were American, recent and measured, but they lasted six months, and people do not reorganize their working lives around a payment they expect to end. Canada's benefit is permanent, recent and measured, but Canada's labour market, health care and other benefits differ. The Mothers' Pensions were permanent and American and measured a lifetime, but a century ago. And the simulation is permanent, American and current, but its key numbers are assumed. No study ticks every box. The memo has to combine them, and say how.
Island: Chapter eight. The policy run on the Island.

Now the analysis the memo rests on: a microsimulation, the method Guy Orcutt proposed in 1957, which applies the rules of a policy to each family one by one. The Island's forty thousand families start under the old credit, calibrated so that eighty-five percent of single parents work and ninety-five percent of couples' main earners. For each parent the simulation computes what working adds to the family's income, under each system. Whether they work depends on that reward through a logistic curve, whose slope is set so that the average participation elasticity is the dial's value, a quarter to begin with. Then incomes, poverty and the cost follow. Every family uses the same random draws under both systems, so the comparison is like for like: no difference is noise.

The results. Under the old credit, 14.3 percent of the Island's children are poor. If no family changed what it did, the allowance would bring that to 10.1 percent, 29 percent fewer poor children. This is the static arithmetic, the kind of number a first headline uses. But at an elasticity of a quarter, 633 parents stop working, 1.7 percent of those who worked. Their families lose earnings and earned income credits, and some of them fall below the line. With responses, child poverty is 11.6 percent: 19 percent fewer poor children, about two thirds of the static fall. Your forecast from chapter four: if you chose a tenth to a quarter, you were right; if you anchored on the 2021 headline of almost half, the difference is the measure, the year's other aid, and the responses a permanent policy would bring.

Who stops working? Not only the lowest earners. Under the old credit a family needed earnings to receive any of it, and enough earnings to receive all of it; so for parents who could earn anywhere up to about forty thousand dollars, the allowance cuts the reward for working by roughly a tenth, and about two to three percent of them stop. Above that the cut is smaller, and fewer stop. And single parents, a third of families, are 74 percent of those who stop, because for them working is a closer call: they have no second earner, and more of them are near the margin.

But the elasticity is uncertain, so the memo cannot rest on a quarter. Run it across the whole range of the dial. The old credit's poverty rate stays where it is. The allowance's rises with the elasticity: 10.1 percent if no one responds, 13.5 percent at an elasticity of a half, where 1,391 parents stop working. Across the whole range the allowance leaves fewer children in poverty than the old credit. The size of the fall depends on the dial; its direction does not.

One number does change sign, and the memo must report it. Deep poverty: children whose families have less than half the poverty line. Under the old credit, 7.8 percent. Under the allowance, 6.4 percent if no one responds, but rising faster with the elasticity, and above an elasticity of about 0.22, higher than under the old credit. The reason is the parents who stop working: they give up their earnings and their earned income credit, and an allowance of a few thousand dollars does not replace them. A single parent of two who stops working lands below half the line. This is exactly the finding the simulation of chapter seven emphasized, and it is why the elasticity matters so much.
Value: Chapter nine. The cost, and the value of public funds.

Now the value of a dollar, with Part forty-two's yardstick: the marginal value of public funds, what recipients would pay for the policy divided by its net cost to the government. What would families pay? By the envelope theorem, as in Part forty-two, the payment itself: the parents who stop working were close to indifferent, so their change of plans adds nothing to the value. That is 108.9 million dollars a year. The cost to the budget is 109.2 million. Without any return later, the ratio is 1.00: a dollar spent delivers a dollar of value, no more and no less. But if the children grow up healthier and better educated and pay more tax as adults, part of the cost comes back. If a quarter of it returns, in today's money, the ratio is 1.33; if half, 1.99. The Island cannot measure that return; it is planted as a range, because the evidence of chapter seven is too old and too indirect to pin it down.

Now combine the two unknowns: how much the children later repay, and how the money is raised. Down the side, the share of the cost that children's later taxes repay: nothing, a quarter, half. Across the top, the cost of raising a dollar: one dollar if it costs nothing extra, 1.33 or 1.67 if it comes from a top surtax, from chapter six. Each cell is the value delivered to families per dollar that the people paying for it give up. With nothing repaid and a surtax, the allowance delivers seventy-five or sixty cents of value per dollar taken. With half repaid, it delivers more than it takes, whichever way it is financed. So the answer turns on a number the evidence cannot yet supply, and on a judgment the evidence never will.

Where do the numbers stop? Take the cell with nothing repaid and a surtax at an elasticity of a quarter: 0.75 dollars of value per dollar taken. The allowance is worth doing if a dollar to a family below the line is worth at least 1.34 dollars to a top earner. That is Nathaniel Hendren's way of comparing policies: the value per dollar of the spending against the value per dollar of the tax that pays for it. The economist can supply the numbers on both sides, and how uncertain they are. The weight a society puts on a poor child's dollar is not an economic finding. It belongs to the minister, and to the voters, and the memo should say so in as many words.
Gainers: Chapter ten. Who gains, and who loses.

Who gains? Rank the Island's families by their income under the old credit, and cut them into ten equal groups. The poorest tenth gains most: 5,467 dollars a year on average, more than the whole of their income before, because many of them had little or no earnings and so little or none of the old credit. The gain falls through the second and third tenths, as the old credit phases in, and in the middle it settles at fourteen to eighteen hundred dollars, the difference between the old and new amounts per child. The richest tenth gains only 452 dollars, because the extra is phased out above seventy-five thousand for a single parent and a hundred and fifty thousand for a couple.

And who loses? On the Island, 1.6 percent of families end up with less income: the families of the 633 parents who stop working. By their own lights they are not worse off, since they chose to stop, and nothing forced them. But their children did not choose, and some of them fall below half the line, as chapter eight showed. A memo that cares about children cannot simply defer to the parents' choice. The taxpayers lose whatever they pay: top earners under a surtax, or later taxpayers if the money is borrowed. And families without children gain nothing directly, and pay their share.

Here the memo reaches the step from is to ought. What is: child poverty falls by about a fifth; the poorest families gain the most; a few parents stop working; and if many did, deep poverty could rise. What the step needs: a judgment about how much a dollar to a poor child should count against a dollar to the person who pays for it, and whether help for children should depend on what their parents do. People who agree on every number in this film can disagree here, and neither side is making an error of economics. And what follows: pay the allowance, pay it with a work requirement, or spend the money another way.
Uncertainty: A memo's most useful page says how sure it is, and what would change its advice. The tool is a tornado chart: move one dial at a time across its range, holding the others at their central values, and draw how far the answer moves. The central estimate of child poverty under the allowance is 11.6 percent; the old credit's is 14.3. The participation elasticity moves the answer most, by more than three points across its range. An income effect on work, which the central case leaves out, moves it by about one. Take-up below a hundred percent, by less than one. And every bar stays to the left of the old credit. The direction of the answer survives every dial; its size does not.

The same for the cost. Here take-up dominates: if only eighty-five percent of families claim, the cost per child falls by about two hundred dollars. The elasticity and the income effect barely move it, for the reason chapter six gave: the parents who stop working paid little tax. So the budget line of the memo is the firmest number in it, and the poverty line the least firm.

So: what would change the advice? A memo should name the switching points. If parents respond strongly to a permanent allowance, with an elasticity above about 0.22, deep poverty rises, and a design that keeps a small phase-in for the extra amount becomes attractive. If little of the cost comes back in children's later taxes and the money comes from a surtax, the allowance delivers 0.75 dollars of value per dollar taken, and the case rests entirely on the weight given to poor children. If the poorest families do not claim, the first task is delivery: paying automatically from records the government already holds, rather than waiting for a tax return. And if research finds the long-run gains that the old evidence suggests, the allowance pays for itself, whatever the weights.
Memo: Now the memo itself, four pages, as the minister asked. A memo is not a paper. It begins with the decision, not the method; every number carries its range; and it separates what the analysis shows from what the minister must judge. Page one, the decision. Page two, what the policy does. Page three, what it costs and what it is worth. Page four, what we do not know.

Page one, the decision. The bottom line: the allowance would cut child poverty on the Island by about a fifth, between 5 and 29 percent across the plausible range, at about 1,473 dollars a child a year. There are two designs worth considering. The full allowance does most for the poorest families if parents keep working, as the evidence so far suggests, although at the central elasticity it slightly raises deep poverty. The second keeps the old credit's work requirement and pays only the extra amount unconditionally: it costs a quarter less, leaves 12.2 percent of children poor rather than 11.6, lowers deep poverty, and is safe if parents respond more than expected. The recommendation: if cutting child poverty is the priority, pay the full allowance, automatically and monthly, starting in some places before others so that the work response is measured, and fall back to the second design if many parents leave work.

Page two, what it does. Child poverty falls from 14.3 to 11.6 percent; with no response it would be 10.1, and at the top of the dial 13.5. About 633 of forty thousand parents stop working, between none and 1,391 across the dial. Deep poverty rises slightly at the central value, and more if the response is stronger. The gains are largest for the poorest tenth and smallest for the richest.

Page three. The cost: 109 million dollars a year on the Island, barely changed by families' responses, and lower if take-up is incomplete, but only by missing the families it is for. The value per dollar: one with nothing repaid later, more if children's later taxes repay part of the cost. If it is paid for by a surtax and nothing is repaid, it delivers sixty to seventy-five cents of value per dollar taken, and the case rests on the weight the government gives to poor children's incomes: the minister's judgment, stated as such.

Page four, what we do not know. How parents respond to a permanent allowance. What the children gain over decades: the best evidence is a century old, and the newest trial found no gains by age four. How many of the poorest would claim it. Each of these moves the answer more than any number on page three.
Four pages: the decision, what it does, what it costs and is worth, and what we do not know.

And the oral version, for the two minutes in a corridor when the minister has not read the memo. Minister: it would cut child poverty by about a fifth, for about fifteen hundred dollars a child a year. Few parents would stop working, unless they respond far more than they did in 2021 or in Canada. Whether it is worth it depends on two things: what the children repay later, which nobody yet knows, and how much you value a dollar to a poor child, which only you can decide. If that is your priority, do it, pay it automatically, and measure as you go.

Now your advice from chapter four. Yes, as designed: child poverty falls to 11.6 percent at the central elasticity, but only to 13.5 if parents respond twice as strongly. Yes, with a work requirement kept for the old credit: 12.2 percent, almost whatever parents do, for a quarter less money; it does less for the families with no earnings at all. Yes, but smaller: the cost and the gains shrink together, and the value per dollar barely moves. And no: the right answer if a poor child's dollar counts for little more than a taxpayer's, or if the money has a use with a higher value per dollar. The analysis does not choose for you. It tells you what each choice buys.
Practice: Chapter thirteen. In practice: how memos are used, and misused.

Who writes memos like this, and for whom? Budget offices, such as America's Congressional Budget Office, created in 1974, which estimate what a bill costs, year by year, over a ten-year window. Tax analysts, who estimate revenue and who pays it, by income group. Regulators, who weigh costs and benefits under written guidance: America's Circular A-4, Britain's Green Book. Ministries and think tanks, who write memos for and against a policy, often from the same numbers. And evaluators, who test a policy after it starts, when it is designed so that it can be tested.

And how do memos go wrong? Six ways, each of which this film has tried to avoid. The window: a policy made temporary so that its cost within the window looks small. The 2021 credit was enacted for a single year. One number: a point estimate with no range, read as a fact. The chosen dial: an elasticity picked for the answer it gives, by supporters or by opponents. Static or dynamic: a cost that ignores behaviour, or one that assumes far more of it than the evidence supports. The missing table: an average gain that hides who loses. And the hidden judgment: a value judgment, such as the weight on poor children's incomes, dressed as a finding.

Called it? A forecast about this very policy. In September 2021, while the monthly payments were arriving, Kevin Corinth, Bruce Meyer, Matthew Stadnicki and Derek Wu forecast that a permanent allowance would lead about 1.5 million working parents to leave work, 2.6 percent of them, and that child poverty would fall by at most 22 percent. The Island's central case is gentler, 1.7 percent. What happened: the temporary payments of 2021 showed no detectable effect on parents' work, and Canada's permanent benefit showed none either. The verdict: too early to say. America has not tried a permanent allowance, and a payment expected to end may not change behaviour as a permanent one would. The forecast was the right question, asked carefully; the evidence that would settle it does not yet exist.
Frontier: Chapter fourteen. Frontier: what remains unidentified.

The frontier for this memo is defined by its weakest page, the long run. The best new evidence is a randomized trial, Baby's First Years. From 2018, 1,000 mothers with incomes below the poverty line were recruited in maternity wards and assigned by lottery to receive either 333 dollars a month, or 20 dollars a month, for the first years of their children's lives. In 2025 the researchers reported the results at age four: no statistically significant effect on any of the four outcomes they had named in advance, language, executive function, social and emotional problems, and brain activity. That is not proof of no effect: the gains of Mothers' Pensions appeared in adulthood, and effects may yet appear later in these children's lives. But it is the most direct modern evidence, and an honest memo must give it the same weight it would give a positive result.

What else remains unidentified? How parents respond to an allowance they expect to last, which a staggered start could measure within a few years. Children's earnings and health as adults: the trials running today will report in the 2040s. Whether a lasting allowance changes births, marriage or who lives with whom. How to pay the poorest families automatically, from records the government already holds. What happens to rents and local prices where many families gain at once. And the weights themselves, which no study identifies: societies reveal them in their budgets and argue about them in their elections. The economist's job is to make that argument about values, and not about facts that could have been measured.
